content: 1. The term Air Handling System refers to equipment designed to introduce outdoor air into a building and remove indoor air, aiming to reduce contaminants in the air and eliminate those generated during the use of aquatic venues by bathers. This system includes components that regulate air movement, temperature, humidity, and pressure, ensuring proper air distribution to prevent condensation, corrosion, and stratification. It also maintains acceptable indoor air quality and delivers fresh air to the breathing zone. 2. Agitated Water describes an aquatic venue where mechanical means, such as aquatic features, are used to discharge, spray, or move the water's surface above or below the static water line. If no static water line exists, movement is considered above the deck plane. 3. An Aquatic Facility is a physical location containing one or more aquatic venues and their supporting infrastructure. 4. An Aquatic Feature refers to individual components within an aquatic venue, such as slides, climbing structures, or water-shooting devices. 5. An Aquatic Facility or Aquatic Venue Enclosure is a continuous barrier that surrounds and secures an aquatic facility or venue, preventing unauthorized access. 6. An Aquatic Venue is an artificially constructed or modified natural structure where the public is exposed to water for recreational or therapeutic purposes. These venues are not intended for activities like livestock watering, irrigation, water storage, fishing, or aquatic habitat. Water exposure may occur through contact, ingestion, or aerosolization, even if the structure does not contain standing water. Examples include swimming pools, wave pools, lazy rivers, surf pools, spas, therapy pools, waterslide landing pools, spray pads, and other interactive water venues. 7. Lazy River refers to a water channel of nearly constant depth where water is propelled by pumps or other means to create a river-like flow, transporting bathers along a defined path. It may include play features and is also known as a tubing pool, leisure river, or current channel. 8. A Spa is a structure designed for warm or cold water use, typically for bathing or recreational purposes, where prolonged exposure is not intended. Spas are not usually drained and refilled after each use and may include hydrotherapy, air induction bubbles, and water recirculation. 9. A Special Use Aquatic Venue refers to aquatic venues that do not conform to the intended use or design features of other identified aquatic venues or pools. 10. Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas at room temperature with a penetrating and irritating smell. It is highly toxic and can be compressed into liquid form for storage in steel tanks. When mixed with water, chlorine gas forms hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the primary disinfecting agent, along with hypochlorite ion and hydrochloric acid. The effectiveness of HOCl as a bactericide is highly pH-dependent, with greater efficacy at lower pH levels. Chlorine is a general term encompassing HOCl and hypochlorite ion in aqueous solutions derived from chlorine gas or other chlorine-based disinfectants. 11. Available Chlorine refers to the reactive, oxidized form of chlorine in the +1 oxidation state, as opposed to the inert, reduced chloride ion (Cl-). Available chlorine is divided into Free Available Chlorine and Combined Available Chlorine. Pool chemicals containing available chlorine act as both oxidizers and disinfectants. Elemental chlorine (Cl2) is defined as containing 100% available chlorine. The concentration of available chlorine in water is typically reported in mg/L (ppm) as Cl2. The pH of the water determines the relative amounts of HOCl and hypochlorite ion, with HOCl being the more effective bactericide. 12. A Circulation Path is a designated pedestrian passageway within an aquatic facility, including walkways, pathways, decks, and stairways, and must comply with ADA requirements. 13. A Cleaning Shower is a shower located within a hygiene facility that uses warm water and soap to remove contaminants such as fecal material, sweat, skin cells, personal care products, and dirt before bathers enter the aquatic venue. 14. A Code is a systematic statement of laws, often given statutory force. 15. A Contamination Response Plan outlines procedures for handling contamination from formed stool, diarrheal stool, vomit, and blood. 16. Corrosive Materials include pool chemicals, fertilizers, cleaning agents, oxidizing materials, salts, de-icing chemicals, pesticides, and other substances that may cause injury or damage to people, buildings, or equipment through direct contact or fumes. Labels and SDS forms should be consulted for safety information. 17. A Crack refers to any break in the structural shell of a pool vessel or deck. 18. A Cross-Connection is a connection or arrangement between a potable water supply system and a plumbing fixture, tank, or device that could allow nonpotable, used, or contaminated water to enter the potable water system under certain conditions. 19. A CT Inactivation Value represents the concentration of a disinfectant (C) multiplied by the time in minutes (T) required to inactivate a specific contaminant. The CT value is inversely proportional to the disinfectant concentration and may vary with pH or temperature changes. 20. A Deck refers to surface areas serving the aquatic venue, including dry decks, perimeter decks, and pool decks. 21. A Diaper-Changing Station includes a diaper-changing unit, hand-washing sink, soap dispenser, hand-drying means, trash receptacle, and disinfectant products for cleaning after use. 22. Dry Deck refers to pedestrian surface areas within the aquatic venue enclosure that are not frequently splashed or subjected to constant wet foot traffic. 23. Emergency Action Plan (EAP) identifies objectives, responders, roles, and required equipment for specific emergencies. 24. An Enclosure is a continuous constructed feature or obstacle designed to secure an area and prevent unauthorized access. It is resistant to climbing and passage. 25. EPA Registered refers to products regulated and registered under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) by the EPA, with a registration number on the label. 26. An Equipment Room or Area is a space for operating pool pumps, filters, heaters, and controllers, not intended for storing hazardous pool chemicals. 27. An Exit Gate is an emergency exit allowing free egress at all times. 28. An Expansion Joint is a watertight joint in a pool vessel that relieves stress caused by thermal expansion or contraction. 29. Flat Water describes an aquatic venue with a static water line, except for movement caused by users. 30. A Flume is the riding channel of a waterslide, accommodating riders with or without mats, tubes, or rafts. 31. Foot Baths are standing water areas where bathers or staff rinse their feet. 32. Free Chlorine Residual or Free Available Chlorine refers to the active disinfecting agent in pool water. 33. A Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) is a device that de-energizes an electrical circuit in the event of excessive ground current. 34. A Hand Wash Station includes a sink, soap dispenser, hand-drying device or paper towels, and a trash receptacle. 35. Hot Water refers to aquatic venues with water temperatures exceeding 90°F (30°C). 36. A Hygiene Facility contains toilets, showers, diaper-changing units, hand wash stations, and dressing areas for bathers and patrons. 37. Hygiene Fixtures include all components necessary for hygiene facilities, such as plumbing fixtures, diaper-changing stations, hand wash stations, trashcans, soap dispensers, and hand dryers. 38. An Imminent Health Hazard is a significant health threat requiring immediate correction or cessation of operation to prevent injury. 39. An Indoor Aquatic Facility is a structure containing aquatic venues and surrounding areas for bathers and spectators, meeting the definition of a Building per the 2012 International Building Code (IBC). 40. An Infinity Edge is a pool wall and adjacent deck designed to create the illusion of water extending to the horizon. Water flows over the edge, is captured, and treated for reuse. 41. An Inlet is a wall or floor fitting where treated water is returned to the pool. 42. An Interactive Water Play Aquatic Venue includes installations with sprayed or jetted water that contacts bathers but does not incorporate standing or captured water. These venues are also known as splash pads or spray pads. 43. Interior Space refers to a substantially enclosed area with a roof and walls that reduce the free flow of outdoor air. 44. An Island is a structure inside a pool, completely surrounded by water, with its top above the water surface. 45. A Landing Pool is an aquatic venue or section designed to receive bathers exiting waterslide flumes. 46. A Lazy River is a water channel with a near-constant depth, propelled by pumps to create a river-like flow. 47. A Lifeguard Supervisor oversees lifeguard performance and emergency response at an aquatic facility. 48. mg/L means milligrams per liter, equivalent to parts per million (ppm). 49. Monitor refers to the regular observation and recording of system or facility data, including alerts and excursions from acceptable ranges. 50. Moveable Floors are pool floors with adjustable depth controlled by mechanisms. 51. A No Diving Marker is a sign with the words No Diving and a universal symbol indicating the prohibition of diving. 52. Noise Criterion is a single-number rating sensitive to loudness and speech interference properties of a noise spectrum. 53. Oxidation is the process of chemically altering water contaminants to make them more removable or soluble. 54. Oxidation Reduction Potential (ORP) measures a solution's tendency to gain or lose electrons, with higher values indicating a more oxidative solution. 55. A Patron is any person at an aquatic facility, whether or not they have contact with the water. 56. A Peninsula/Wing Wall is a structural projection into a pool that provides separation within the water body. 57. A Perimeter Gutter System is an alternative to skimmers for removing water from the pool's surface. 58. A Plumbing Fixture is a device connected to a water supply or drainage system, such as toilets, urinals, and showers. 59. pH measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in water, indicating its acidity or alkalinity. 60. A Pool is a subset of aquatic venues designed for standing water and bather immersion. 61. An Activity Pool is a water attraction primarily for play, using constructed features and devices. 62. A Diving Pool is used exclusively for diving. 63. A Landing Pool is designed to receive bathers exiting waterslide flumes. 64. A Skimmer Pool uses a skimmer system. 65. A Surf Pool generates waves for surfing activities. 66. A Therapy Pool is used exclusively for aquatic therapy or rehabilitation under professional supervision. 67. A Wave Pool simulates breaking or cyclic waves for general play. 68. A Pool Deck refers to surface areas serving the aquatic venue. 69. A Pool Slide is a slide allowing users to descend from an elevated height into a pool. 70. A Public Water System includes community and non-community water systems regulated by the EPA. 71. Recessed Steps are steps recessed into the pool wall for ingress/egress. 72. A Recirculation System combines components to circulate pool water to and from treatment systems. 73. Re-entrainment occurs when exhaust air from a ventilated source is recaptured by the air handling system. 74. A Responsible Supervisor oversees water treatment operations when a qualified operator is not on-site. 75. A Rinse Shower is a shower typically located on the pool deck to remove dirt and organic material before entering the aquatic venue. 76. A Skimmer is a device installed in the pool wall to remove floating debris and surface water. 77. A Slide is an aquatic feature where users slide down from an elevated height into water. 78. A Sound Absorption property allows materials or structures to dissipate sound energy. 79. Superchlorination involves adding large quantities of chlorine-based chemicals to kill algae, eliminate odors, or improve disinfectant residual maintenance.
